*   **Time Complexity**: The method requires computing screen-space derivatives and then iterating over all Gabor kernels.
For each kernel, it performs matrix inversions and multiplications to update the parameters.
The complexity is $O(N)$ per pixel, where $N$ is the number of kernels.

*   **Measured Performance**: Performance depends on the number of kernels and the cost of evaluating the Gabor function.

*   **When Not to Use**: Avoid if the noise is isotropic and the surface is viewed front-on, as simpler filtering methods may suffice.
Gabor Noise was introduced by Goldberg et al. [GZD08] in 2008 as a noise function that supports high-quality anisotropic filtering by tiling the frequency domain into oriented subbands.
The analytical filtering method for Gabor noise was described by Lagae et al. [LLDD09a] in 2009, exploiting the property that Gabor kernels correspond to Gaussians in the frequency domain.
This allows for direct generation of filtered noise by modifying kernel parameters, avoiding the need for explicit convolution or discretization of the spectrum.
